text:
GitHub Copilot CLI shipped an undo button. That changes who's willing to let an agent near their code.

What changed: the CLI added /rewind. It restores the changes Copilot made without needing git, and it leaves the edits you made yourself in place. It also added an experimental /worktree that spins the agent into an isolated workspace, and it now queues your prompts and shell commands while it's still working.

What it actually does: it makes an agent's work reversible at the file level. You're no longer choosing between letting it run and keeping your repo safe. Hand it a real task, read the result properly, and put the whole thing back in one command if you don't like it.

Why builders should care: the thing stopping most people was never the model's ability. It's the fear of damage. Cheap undo is what turns an experiment into a habit.

Try this this week: pick one file you'd normally protect. Let the agent rewrite it end to end. Read it. Then rewind it whether it was good or not, just to feel how cheap reversing it is. Do that once and you'll stop hedging your prompts.

The bigger signal: agent tooling has stopped competing on raw output and started competing on control. Sandboxes, worktrees, queues, rewinds. The model was never the hard part. Trust was.

Save this for your AI stack.

text:
English is the new form of code. Here's how to write a sentence a model can actually act on.

That line came off Tech Thursday last week, and the proof was on screen ten minutes later. "Recreate this flyer" gave us a brochure. "Recreate this flyer, make it social media ready" gave us a post. Two words. Completely different output.

The model already knows what a social post looks like. It knows what a brochure looks like. It just doesn't know which room you're standing in.

So name it. Five things, one plain sentence:

1. The format. Social media ready, 9:16, a carousel, a one-pager. Say it first.
2. The audience. Who reads it and where they'll see it.
3. The one action. One call to action, not four. Nobody's reading four.
4. Fewer words on the image. The simpler the wording, the less the model has to get wrong.
5. What done looks like. Describe the finished thing, not the steps to make it.

That's the whole gap between "this doesn't work" and "this works wonders."

Comment BUILD and I'll send you the workflow map.
